briefing.title: Build a Simple Expense Tracker
text: You'll build a program that records what you spend, adds it up, groups it by category and checks it against a budget.
You build it one piece at a time. At each step you choose the right line of code, and it appears in the program.
This program does not use input(). To track your own spending, change the add_expense(...) lines and run it again in the Practical tab.
why: Knowing where your money goes is the first step to saving
Real apps such as banking and shopping apps do the same: store records, total them, group them
It combines functions, lists, dictionaries, loops and f-strings in one useful program
briefing.sampleOutput:
=== Expense Report ===
Lunch      Rs  120
Bus pass   Rs  300
Notebook   Rs   80
Dinner     Rs  250
Movie      Rs  200
--- By category ---
Food: Rs 370
Travel: Rs 300
Other: Rs 80
Fun: Rs 200
Total spent: Rs 950
Big expenses: Bus pass, Dinner, Movie
Left to spend: Rs 1050

finalCode: big = [e["name"] for e in expenses if e["amount"] >= 200]

stages.instruction: Every tracker needs a budget and somewhere to keep the expenses. The budget is ready; now create an empty list for the expenses.

question.prompt: Which line creates an empty list to collect expenses?
question.explanation: [] is an empty list. Lists keep items in order and let you append() new ones (5.1).

optionFeedback: That's an empty string. Strings have no append() method.
{} is an empty dictionary. We want an ordered list we can append() to.

question.explanation: Parameters with defaults go last, so category="Other" comes after name and amount (4.4).

stages.instruction: Now a function that adds up every amount. It needs a running total that starts at zero, then a loop over all expenses.

stages.title: Totals per category
stages.instruction: Next, a function that works out how much was spent in each category. Start it with the right empty container for name-to-total pairs.

question.explanation: A dictionary maps each category name to its total, like {"Food": 370} (6.3).

stages.title: Count with get()
stages.instruction: For each expense, add its amount to the running total for its category. The first time a category appears it has no total yet.

question.prompt: Which line updates the category total safely?
question.explanation: get(category, 0) gives 0 for a new category, then the amount is added and stored (6.3 counting pattern).

optionFeedback: The first time a category appears it isn't a key yet, so this is a KeyError.
get() without a default returns None for a new category, and the result isn't stored.

stages.instruction: Time to use add_expense(). Lunch, Bus pass, Dinner and Movie each have a category. The notebook doesn't, so it should go into "Other".

question.prompt: Which call adds the notebook using the default category?
question.explanation: Leaving out the category makes Python use the default "Other" (4.4).

optionFeedback: Leaving out the category makes Python use the default "Other" (4.4).

stages.title: Print the report
stages.instruction: Print a heading, then one neat line per expense: the name left-aligned in 10 spaces and the amount right-aligned in 4.

question.prompt: Which line prints each expense neatly?
question.explanation: :<10 left-aligns the name in 10 spaces and :>4 right-aligns the amount (6.2).

optionFeedback: The alignments are swapped: names would be pushed right and amounts left.
Without the f, the braces are printed as plain text.
:<10 left-aligns the name in 10 spaces and :>4 right-aligns the amount (6.2).

stages.instruction: Print a second heading, then loop over the dictionary returned by totals_by_category(), taking each category and its amount.

question.explanation: Call the function with (), then .items() gives key-value pairs to unpack (6.4).

stages.title: Total and big expenses
stages.instruction: Store the total, then build a list of the NAMES of expenses of 200 or more, and print both. join() turns the names into one line.

question.prompt: Which line builds the list of big expense names?
options: big = [e["name"] for e in expenses if e["amount"] >= 200]
big = [e["name"] for e in expenses if e >= 200]
big = [for e in expenses e["name"] if e["amount"] >= 200]
big = [e for e in expenses if e["amount"] >= 200]
question.explanation: Value first, then for, then the filter: a simple list comprehension (5.5).

optionFeedback: Value first, then for, then the filter: a simple list comprehension (5.5).

stages.title: Check the budget
stages.instruction: Finally, compare what was spent with the budget and tell the user how it went.

question.prompt: What should the program do here?
options: Use break to stop the program when spent is more than budget
Set spent back to 0 so the budget is never exceeded
Print the budget without comparing it to spent
If spent is more than budget, print "Over budget!", otherwise print how much is left
question.explanation: An if/else picks one of two messages (2.2). 2000 - 950 leaves Rs 1050.

optionFeedback: break only works inside a loop, and stopping wouldn't tell the user anything.
That throws away the real total and hides the problem.
The user wants to know how spending compares with the budget, not just the budget.
An if/else picks one of two messages (2.2). 2000 - 950 leaves Rs 1050.

walkthrough: Lines 2-3 create the budget and an empty list. Each expense will be a dictionary inside that list.
add_expense() builds a dictionary from its parameters and appends it. category defaults to "Other".
total_spent() starts at 0, adds every amount in a loop and returns the result.
totals_by_category() uses get(category, 0) so a new category starts at 0, then adds to it.
The five add_expense(...) calls fill the list. Notebook has no category, so it uses "Other".
The report loops over the list and uses :<10 and :>4 to line the columns up.
items() gives each category with its total. The list comprehension picks the names of expenses of 200 or more.
Finally if/else compares spent with budget: 950 is under 2000, so Rs 1050 is left.
